title: Whole Hospital Bed Occupancy Explained: Why Do Countries Operate at Different Average Bed Occupancy and to Which Specific Context Does 85% Occupancy Apply?
content: Whole hospital bed occupancy is explained based on the size of the individual units/departments within each hospital. The weighted population density and the deaths per 1000 population combine to influence the size distribution of hospitals (WPD) within a country/region. This explains why different countries and regions operate at different average occupancy. It also explains why smaller hospitals must operate at lower average occupancy to avoid access block. Mixed specialty hospitals in the USA operate at around 76% (upper quartile 81%) occupancy at 1000 beds, 68% (75%) at 500, 55% (64%) at 100 and 32% (40%) at 20 beds, etc. However, single function/specialty hospitals tend to have an occupancy lying between the 0.1% to 3% lines of turn-away as calculated by the Erlang equation. The often-quoted figure of 85% occupancy is used as an approximate measure of daily busyness/workload and will occur most often in larger hospitals where most studies of this nature are conducted. For example, in 2025 some 12% of a sample (n = 107) of 500+ bed US hospitals operated above 85% annual average occupancy (midnight). Above this figure the workload becomes such that medication errors, falls, hospital acquired infection (HAI) and stress occur in increasing measures. Attribution of cause and effect is clouded because above 85% both busyness and delays to admission (access block) can often occur simultaneously. Acute bed occupancy in England follows a trajectory where the entire acute NHS could be at 100% occupancy by 2040. This is the result of serious failures in bed planning by successive governments over the past 30 years. Increasing numbers of same day stay admissions are causing underestimation of the real levels of bed occupancy. Hence, the apparent higher US bed occupancy in the 1960’s to 80’s (76.5 ± 1.7% vs 66.2 ± 0.2% since the 2000’s) may reflect something closer to real time bed occupancy in the earlier years. The situation and consequences in the USA for increasing post-pandemic occupancy can be explained in the above context with lessons to be learned from England.
